zh.text:
各种光学仪器的构造和作用都以几何光学定律为基础，本课先研究形成实像的情况。
在感光片或胶卷摄影中，利用光的化学作用记录这个像，再经过定影等处理把它保存下来。
这里的化学记录过程指感光材料摄影，不是数字相机的电子记录方式。

按照原书的历史概述，摄影是在 19 世纪 30 年代发明的，随后走过了漫长的发展道路。
摄影技术逐渐实现了小型化、快速拍摄、彩色摄影和立体摄影，并广泛应用于生活的各个领域。
它在研究自然界时也有重要作用：既能记录微观物体，也能记录宇宙中的物体，还能记录不可见的辐射。
艺术摄影具有重要意义。
电影也是摄影技术在艺术中的一种发展。

被摄物体可以位于离照相机不同的距离处。
在薄透镜近似下，物距改变时，清晰实像的位置也会改变，因此需要相应调整镜头到感光片或胶卷的距离。
原书举出的做法是利用螺纹机构移动镜头，或让暗箱伸缩。
伸缩暗箱做成像“手风琴”一样的皮腔。
这些做法说明了调焦的原理，并不表示所有相机都靠整个镜头平移来调焦。

**投影仪** 用来在屏幕上获得物体放大的实像。
被投影的物体可以是从后面照明的透明图片或幻灯片，图 183 是这种仪器的结构简图。
镜头 $O$ 在屏幕上形成幻灯片 $D$ 的像。

称为聚光器的透镜组 $K$ 把光源发出的光集中到幻灯片上，负责照亮幻灯片；
物镜负责把被照亮的幻灯片成像在屏幕上。
图中展示了光从幻灯片经镜头到达屏幕的光路。
在薄透镜、近轴模型中，要用会聚物镜得到放大的实像，幻灯片应位于焦距和两倍焦距之间。
屏幕应放在相应的实像位置。

不透明物体也可以像透明物体一样，被投影成像在屏幕上。
用于这种投影的仪器叫作反射映画器。
例如，要把书上的插图投影到屏幕上，需要用很强的光照亮插图，再由镜头把插图成像在屏幕上。
这里进入镜头的是物体反射的光。
它不是穿过不透明物体的光。

en.text:
The construction and operation of optical instruments are based on geometrical optics.
We first consider instruments that form real images.
Light acts chemically to record an image on photosensitive plates or film.
The image is then fixed and preserved.
Digital cameras record electronically, not by this chemical process.

The textbook dates photography's invention to the nineteenth century's thirties (century 19, decade 30).
Photography then followed a long path of development.
It became compact and fast, with color and stereoscopic techniques, and found wide use in everyday life.
Photography is also important in the study of nature.
It can record objects from microscopic to astronomical scales, as well as invisible radiation.
Artistic photography is significant, and cinema developed from it as an art form.

**Camera** Figure 181 shows a camera used as an example in the textbook.
Its main parts are a light-tight box and a group of lenses called the objective.
The simplest objective is a single converging lens.
In the thin-lens, paraxial approximation, the objective forms an inverted real image near the back wall of the box.
The object is usually beyond twice the objective's focal length, so its image is reduced.
At the image plane is a photosensitive plate or film coated with photographic emulsion.

Objects being photographed can be at different distances from the camera.
In the thin-lens approximation, changing the object distance changes the position of the sharp real image.
The objective-to-plate or objective-to-film distance must therefore be adjusted accordingly.
The textbook uses threaded objective motion or an extensible light-tight accordion bellows.
These examples explain focusing.
These examples do not imply that every camera focuses by translating the whole objective.

The shutter admits light for an exposure time, controlling energy reaching the photosensitive layer.
The required time depends on emulsion sensitivity and film irradiance.
Compare images in paraxial geometrical optics.
Keep object radiance and lens transmission the same.
Film irradiance rises with a larger effective opening.
Film irradiance also rises with a shorter image-side distance from the objective to the photosensitive layer.
This is an image-plane illumination comparison.
Focusing distance alone does not universally determine exposure.
The aperture sets effective lens diameter and film irradiance.
It also affects sharpness at different object distances.

Suppose the camera is focused on a luminous point $A$ at a particular distance.
In the ideal thin-lens, paraxial geometrical-optics model, its film image is a point (Figure 182a).
Point $B$ (Figure 182b) is nearer, and point $C$ (Figure 182c) is farther.
Both form small defocus circles on that same film plane.
An aperture is placed before the objective (Figure 182d, e, f).
A smaller effective opening gives smaller defocus circles (Figure 182e, f).
Stopping down makes a range of object distances look sufficiently sharp: depth of field increases.
Sufficient sharpness does not put all objects in exact focus on the same plane.
Sufficient sharpness need not make every defocus circle a mathematical point.
This holds where geometrical defocus dominates.
At very small apertures, diffraction also blurs the image.
Real lenses also have aberrations.
The ideal image point does not imply exact concurrence for arbitrary ray angles or finite apertures.

**Projector** A projector forms an enlarged real image of an object on a screen.
The object can be a transparent picture or slide illuminated from behind.
Figure 183 shows the arrangement.
The objective $O$ forms an image of the slide $D$ on the screen.
The lens group $K$, called the condenser, concentrates light from the source onto the slide.
The condenser lights the slide, while the objective images it on the screen.
The diagram shows the light path from the slide through the objective to the screen.
Consider the thin-lens, paraxial model.
For an enlarged real image, the slide must lie between one and two focal lengths from the converging objective.
The screen must be at the corresponding real-image position.

Change magnification by moving the objective toward or away from the slide.
At the same time, change the projector-to-screen distance.
In the fixed-focal-length thin-lens model, object and image distances must be adjusted together.
This keeps the screen at the sharp real-image position.
Suppose only the objective moves while the screen is held at an arbitrary fixed position.
This does not guarantee a sharp enlarged image.

Opaque objects, like transparent ones, can also be imaged on a screen by projection.
An instrument for this is an opaque projector, or episcope.
This name corresponds to the source term for reflected-light projection.
To project a book illustration, illuminate it strongly and image it on the screen with the objective.
Light enters the objective after reflection from the opaque object.
It is not transmitted through that object.
